headline: A rough day across most of your portfolio as tech stocks sold off and Pilbara Minerals copped a 6% hammering, while Google's new Gemini 4 Argon AI model arrives just ahead of a big earnings date.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara got belted again today, down 6.3% at the close. Lithium chemicals like lithium hexafluorophosphate have been weakening through October — prices were flat early in the month then slipped mid-month, and that's dragging lithium miners down with them. No company-specific news, just the ongoing pain from depressed lithium prices globally.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: The AI ETF dropped 4.7% today, tracking a big sell-off in global tech last night — the NASDAQ fell nearly 2%. Google and Microsoft (two major holdings in AI-focused ETFs) both slid, pulling the whole basket lower. No structural change to the AI investment story here, just broad tech weakness.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft slipped 1.8% last night as the NASDAQ had a rough session. Bloomberg has been running a bullish piece on Microsoft and AI investment, so no bad news on the company itself — this looks like broad market profit-taking rather than anything Microsoft-specific.

movers.name: Alphabet (Google)
movers.note: Google fell 1.7% last night, slightly more than the broader market. This comes even as Google launched its new Gemini 4 Argon AI model — the dip seems to be general tech weakness rather than bad news. Motley Fool analysts are predicting the stock will bounce after October 28 earnings, which is the next big catalyst to watch.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: Emerging markets dipped 1.1% today, dragged lower by a softer Aussie dollar (down about 1% against the USD) and general global risk-off sentiment. Middle East tensions and concerns about global economic fragility flagged by the IMF are weighing on riskier assets.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS fell 0.9% today on the ASX, reflecting last night's Wall Street sell-off where the S&P 500 dropped 1.1% and the NASDAQ fell nearly 2%. US markets had a tough night driven by tech weakness — but as a broad market ETF, the long-term story here is unchanged.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG edged down 0.67% today, a modest dip reflecting the global tech weakness filtering through its international equity component. As a diversified fund across asset classes and geographies, it's cushioned from the worst of the tech sell-off.

movers.name: DHHF
movers.note: DHHF slipped a very small 0.55% today — essentially flat. As a broad global shares ETF, it's well-diversified and this is just everyday market noise.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two was one of the few green spots last night, up 0.45% even as the broader market fell. GTA 6 buzz is clearly helping — Bloomberg ran a big behind-the-scenes piece on the making of GTA VI, and reports suggest a PC release could land in early 2027. Rockstar also said future games will come out faster now that the GTA 6 engine and tools are built. Good news for the long-term thesis.

watch_today.title: Pilbara Minerals: Down 6% today — long-term thesis under pressure
watch_today.detail: PLS.AX closed at $2.97, down another 6.3% today and now sitting at a massive 55.9% loss on your investment. Lithium prices continue to weaken globally with no clear floor in sight. This one is painful to hold but the investment case depends entirely on a lithium price recovery — if you still believe in that long-term story, sitting tight is defensible. But it's worth asking yourself honestly: has anything changed your view on when lithium demand picks up?

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX: AI ETF down 4.7% today — hold through the tech noise
watch_today.detail: The Global X AI ETF dropped sharply today on broad tech weakness, and is now down 12.6% overall on your investment. However, Google literally launched a major new AI model (Gemini 4 Argon) today, and the AI investment story is anything but dead. This is volatility, not a structural break. For a long-term holder, sit tight.

watch_today.title: Google earnings on October 28 — key date for GOOG holders
watch_today.detail: GOOG fell 1.7% last night but is still up 11.8% on your total investment. The real event to watch is earnings on October 28 (US time) — Motley Fool analysts are bullish heading in, citing AI momentum and the just-launched Gemini 4 Argon model. Nothing broken in the long-term story here. Hold into earnings.

watch_today.title: Take-Two Interactive: Rare green day — GTA 6 buzz building
watch_today.detail: TTWO was up 0.45% last night even as the market sold off, fuelled by Bloomberg's big GTA VI feature and reports of a potential early 2027 PC release. You're still down 6.8% overall on this position, but the long-term catalyst (GTA 6 launch) is intact and getting closer. Rockstar says future games will also come out faster now. Hold — the thesis is playing out.

watch_today.title: US midterm elections underway — watch for market volatility
watch_today.detail: The US midterm elections are in full swing, with significant controversy around the Justice Department pressing California to withhold ballots from flagged voters. Political uncertainty in the US tends to create short-term market jitters. Your US holdings (GOOG, MSFT, TTWO, VTS) could see some extra noise this week. Nothing to act on, just worth being aware of.

watch_today.title: IMF warns global economy is 'precariously poised' — watch emerging markets
watch_today.detail: The IMF this week flagged that declining oil reserves, rising government debt in wealthy nations, and geopolitical tensions are putting the global economy under pressure. This is a headwind for your emerging markets holding (VGE.AX) in particular. Not a reason to sell, but worth keeping an eye on as these macro risks develop.

world.summary: A busy day globally — US midterm elections are causing major controversy, Middle East tensions are escalating with Houthi missile strikes on Riyadh, oil prices are volatile, and the IMF is sounding alarm bells about the global economy.

stories.title: Houthis strike Riyadh as Saudi Arabia faces growing pressure in Yemen conflict
stories.why_it_matters: Houthi rebels from Yemen fired missiles that struck Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's capital, and have pledged to keep targeting Saudi airports and oil facilities. Saudi Arabia is in open conflict with the Houthis and ABC News reports the Saudis face a 'huge problem' — they can't easily stop the missile attacks, and their oil infrastructure is exposed. Attacks on Hormuz shipping (the narrow strait through which a huge chunk of the world's oil passes) have hit a wartime high. This matters because disruption to oil supply pushes fuel prices up globally — including at the bowser in Australia.

stories.title: US Justice Department pressures California to withhold ballots as midterms heat up
stories.why_it_matters: With US midterm elections now underway, the Trump administration's Justice Department has moved to pressure California — a Democrat-leaning state — to withhold ballots from voters flagged in a federal database. Critics say this is a politically motivated attempt to suppress votes. Canada says the US is also 'monitoring' it for signs of election interference. Reuters has published a detailed analysis of nine ways the Trump administration could interfere with the midterms. This is a major developing political story with potential consequences for US market stability if results are contested.

stories.title: IMF warns wealthy nations to rein in debt as global economy stays 'precariously poised'
stories.why_it_matters: The IMF (International Monetary Fund — basically the world's financial watchdog) has warned that the global economy remains 'precariously poised' despite some bright spots like India and Germany growing faster than expected. The IMF chief is urging wealthy countries like the US and UK to cut their government debt loads, warning that declining oil reserves and rising debt are real threats to global stability. For Australian investors, this matters because global economic weakness filters through to our exports, share markets, and currency.

stories.title: Middle East conflict pushes oil toward $94 a barrel and reshapes global shipping
stories.why_it_matters: Crude oil (WTI) is trading near $94 a barrel — elevated but slightly off recent highs — as Middle East tensions keep supply fears alive. Interestingly, the conflict is creating new shipping opportunities for African ports as cargo ships reroute away from the Red Sea and Hormuz. Higher oil prices feed into inflation globally, which makes central banks like the RBA more cautious about cutting interest rates — directly relevant to Australian mortgage holders.

stories.title: Attacks on Hormuz shipping hit wartime high
stories.why_it_matters: Attacks on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow waterway connecting the Persian Gulf to the open ocean, through which about 20% of the world's oil flows — have reached their highest level since the current Middle East conflict began. This is a serious escalation. If the strait were significantly disrupted, global oil and gas prices would spike sharply, hitting fuel costs and inflation worldwide, including in Australia.

markets.summary: Last night was ugly on Wall Street — the NASDAQ fell nearly 2% and the S&P 500 dropped 1.1%, driven by a tech sell-off. The ASX held up relatively well today, barely budging. Gold surged to over $4,165 USD as investors sought safety, while oil eased slightly despite ongoing Middle East tensions. The Aussie dollar slipped about 1% against the USD.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Essentially flat today — the ASX brushed off Wall Street's weakness, closing down less than 10 points.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: A rough night last night in the US — the S&P fell 1.1% as tech stocks led the sell-off.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: The tech-heavy NASDAQ dropped nearly 2% last night, hit hardest by falls in major names like Google and Microsoft.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil pulled back slightly to around $93.60 a barrel despite ongoing Middle East tensions — still elevated by historical standards.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold jumped 1.4% to over $4,165 USD an ounce as investors piled into safe-haven assets amid geopolitical turmoil.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar fell about 1 US cent to 69.2 cents — partly due to weak jobs data locally and global risk aversion.

politics.summary: A big day for Australian economic data — unemployment hit a five-year high after almost 40,000 jobs were lost, the RBA posted a massive $11.3 billion loss, and there are new battles in Canberra over digital censorship laws and private health insurance.

stories.title: Unemployment hits five-year high after nearly 40,000 jobs lost
stories.why_it_matters: Australia's unemployment rate has climbed to a five-year high after the economy shed close to 40,000 jobs. This is putting real pressure on the RBA (Reserve Bank of Australia) to hold off on any further interest rate rises — and markets are increasingly pricing in rate cuts rather than hikes. For homeowners on variable mortgages, this is actually good news in terms of rate expectations. For the broader economy though, rising unemployment signals the consumer spending squeeze is real and getting worse.

stories.title: RBA books $11.3 billion loss — second biggest on record
stories.why_it_matters: The Reserve Bank of Australia has posted an $11.3 billion loss — the second largest in its history. This comes from the bond purchases it made during COVID to keep interest rates low (called quantitative easing — basically the RBA bought government bonds to pump money into the economy). As rates rose, those bonds fell in value, creating a giant paper loss. The RBA doesn't need to be bailed out and it still functions normally, but it does mean the government won't be receiving any dividend payments from the RBA anytime soon.

stories.title: Labor's Digital Duty of Care bill fires up censorship debate
stories.why_it_matters: The Albanese government's proposed Digital Duty of Care legislation is being slammed as 'radical state censorship' by critics including US commentator Michael Shellenberger, who called it 'insane' and 'absurd'. The bill would impose legal duties on social media platforms to protect users from harmful content. Supporters say it's needed to protect kids online; critics argue it gives government too much power to control what Australians can see online. This is a significant debate about free speech versus online safety that's likely heading for a Senate fight.

stories.title: Greens block Labor's private health insurance rebate cut
stories.why_it_matters: Labor's plan to reduce the government rebate (subsidy) that higher-income earners get on private health insurance has been blocked in the Senate by the Greens, who wanted pensioners carved out from the changes. Without the Greens' votes, Labor can't get the bill through. This matters for the roughly 14 million Australians with private health cover — if the rebate is eventually cut, their premiums could rise further as more people drop private cover and shift to the public system.

ai.summary: Google has officially launched Gemini 4 Argon — its most capable AI model yet — putting it head-to-head with OpenAI's GPT-6 and Anthropic's Claude. It's a big moment for Google, which had been seen as falling behind in the AI race. The AI regulation debate is also heating up in the UK, US, and Australia.

stories.title: Google launches Gemini 4 Argon — finally catching up in the AI race
stories.why_it_matters: Google has publicly released Gemini 4 Argon, described as matching the performance of OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra and Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.1 — the two leading AI models in the world right now. Gemini 4 Argon is specifically designed to excel at coding, research, and reasoning tasks. This is significant because Google had been widely seen as a step behind OpenAI and Anthropic in the AI race; Argon is their attempt to level the playing field. For GOOG shareholders, this is exactly the kind of product moment that supports the long-term investment case.

stories.title: Gemini 4 Argon vs GPT-6 vs Claude — how do they compare?
stories.why_it_matters: Early comparisons show Gemini 4 Argon is genuinely competitive with GPT-6 and Claude Opus 5.5, though Claude is reportedly priced at roughly twice what Argon costs to use via API (the programming interface businesses use to plug AI into their products). For users, this competition is great news — it pushes all three companies to improve their models faster and keeps prices from getting out of hand. For investors in Google, having a model that competes on quality AND price is a strong commercial position.

stories.title: UK's financial regulator plans to use AI to automate financial oversight
stories.why_it_matters: The UK's Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) — the body that regulates banks, brokers, and financial products — has announced plans to use AI to automate parts of financial regulation. Instead of human regulators manually reviewing reports and filings, AI would do much of the scanning and flagging. This is a significant signal that AI is moving from consumer apps into the core machinery of how governments and regulators operate. It also raises questions about accountability — what happens when an AI makes a regulatory mistake?

stories.title: The big debate: Should AI regulation differ for consumers, businesses, and governments?
stories.why_it_matters: Policymakers and tech experts are debating whether AI used by everyday consumers (like chatbots), businesses (like automated hiring tools), and governments (like surveillance or welfare assessment) should each face different rules. The argument is that the risks are very different — a chatbot giving bad advice is annoying, but a government AI denying someone welfare based on a flawed algorithm is a rights issue. This debate will shape the regulatory environment that companies like Google and Microsoft operate in over the next decade.

sport.summary: In NRL news, the Kangaroos got a stunning debut from Jack Bostock, there are big coaching and player movement stories, and the AFL trade period has just wrapped up with some major moves.

stories.title: Jack Bostock bags a hat-trick on Kangaroos debut in flying NRL start
stories.why_it_matters: Jack Bostock scored three tries on his Kangaroos debut, leading the Roos to a victory in what NRL.com is calling a 'flash' performance. It's a remarkable story — Fox Sports detail the setbacks Bostock overcame to get to this point, including injuries and form slumps. His future at international level looks bright, though Fox Sports note his club future remains uncertain.

stories.title: Roosters win NRL Grand Final over Knights 19-18 in thriller
stories.why_it_matters: The NRL Grand Final was played earlier this month at Accor Stadium with the Sydney Roosters defeating the Newcastle Knights 19-18 in what was an absolute nail-biter. Just one point in it at the final whistle — as tight as it gets on rugby league's biggest night.

stories.title: Kain Anderson signs with the Dolphins ahead of 2027 season
stories.why_it_matters: Kain Anderson has officially signed with the Dolphins for the 2027 NRL season. The Dolphins continue to build their roster as the Gold Coast's newest NRL club looks to establish itself as a genuine contender. Worth watching as the local team grows.

stories.title: AFL trade period wraps up: Richmond lands extra top-5 pick, Eagles grab Demons duo
stories.why_it_matters: The AFL Continental Tyres Trade Period has officially closed. Richmond pulled off a nice result, securing an additional top-5 draft pick to help their rebuild. West Coast Eagles grabbed two Melbourne Demons players in what's being described as a significant boost for the Eagles' rebuild. Fox Sports has ranked all 18 clubs by how well they traded — worth a read if your club was active.
